claim: A synaptic active zone (AZ) can release multiple vesicles in response to an action potential.
source: A synaptic active zone (AZ) can release multiple vesicles in response to an action potential.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that is supported by the entire study's experimental data and is consistent with established scientific knowledge about multi-vesicular release.

claim: Multi-vesicular release (MVR) occurs at most synapses.
source: This multi-vesicular release (MVR) occurs at most synapses, but its spatiotemporal properties are unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: There is unprecedented heterogeneity among vesicle release sites within a single AZ, with a gradient of release probability decreasing from AZ center to periphery.
source: Nanoscale-resolution detection of individual release events in hippocampal synapses revealed unprecedented heterogeneity among vesicle release sites within a single AZ, with a gradient of release probability decreasing from AZ center to periphery.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and related analyses.

claim: MVR events preferentially overlap with uni-vesicular release (UVR) events at sites closer to an AZ center.
source: Parallel to this organization, MVR events preferentially overlap with uni-vesicular release (UVR) events at sites closer to an AZ center.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1F and 1G showing spatial overlap patterns.

claim: Pairs of fusion events comprising MVR are not perfectly synchronized.
source: Pairs of fusion events comprising MVR are also not perfectly synchronized, and the earlier event tends to occur closer to AZ center.
evidence: This is supported by amplitude analysis data in Figure 3 showing temporal desynchronization.

claim: The earlier event in MVR pairs tends to occur closer to AZ center.
source: Pairs of fusion events comprising MVR are also not perfectly synchronized, and the earlier event tends to occur closer to AZ center.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figures 3B and 3C showing spatial organization of MVR events.

claim: The spatial features of release sites and MVR events are similarly tightened by buffering intracellular calcium.
source: The spatial features of release sites and MVR events are similarly tightened by buffering intracellular calcium.
evidence: This is supported by EGTA experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The spatiotemporal features of MVR events are controlled, in part, by non-uniform calcium elevation across the AZ.
source: These observations revealed a marked heterogeneity of release site properties within individual AZs, which determines the spatiotemporal features of MVR events and is controlled, in part, by non-uniform calcium elevation across the AZ.
evidence: This conclusion is based on EGTA buffering experiments in Figure 4 and represents an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The initial hypothesis was that, at most, only a single vesicle is released by a given synapse in response to an action potential.
source: Although the initial hypothesis was that, at most, only a single vesicle is released by a given synapse in response to an action potential (i.e., uni-vesicular release (UVR)), we now know that two or more vesicles can be released in response to a single action potential, even within the same synaptic bouton (Rudolph et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a historical statement about the field supported by citation.

claim: Two or more vesicles can be released in response to a single action potential, even within the same synaptic bouton.
source: Although the initial hypothesis was that, at most, only a single vesicle is released by a given synapse in response to an action potential (i.e., uni-vesicular release (UVR)), we now know that two or more vesicles can be released in response to a single action potential, even within the same synaptic bouton (Rudolph et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rudolph et al., 2015 and represents established knowledge.

claim: MVR is a ubiquitous release mechanism, occurring at both small and large central synapses throughout the brain.
source: Indeed, MVR is a ubiquitous release mechanism, occurring at both small and large central synapses throughout the brain (Auger et al., 1998; Christie and Jahr, 2006; Foster et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2010; Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Malagon et al., 2016; Oertner et al., 2002; Rudolph et al., 2011; Singer et al., 2004; Taschenberger et al., 2002; Tong and Jahr, 1994; Wadiche and Jahr, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The vast majority of small central synapses contain only a single active zone (AZ).
source: Because the vast majority of small central synapses contain only a single active zone (AZ) (Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Schikorski and Stevens, 1999), it follows that individual AZs must be capable of supporting both UVR and MVR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schikorski and Stevens studies.

claim: Individual AZs must be capable of supporting both UVR and MVR.
source: Because the vast majority of small central synapses contain only a single active zone (AZ) (Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Schikorski and Stevens, 1999), it follows that individual AZs must be capable of supporting both UVR and MVR.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the cited fact that small synapses have single AZs and the observation that MVR occurs at these synapses.

claim: MVR has been suggested to serve a wide range of functions, including enhancing synaptic reliability, controlling synaptic integration, enhancing efficient information transmission by complex spikes, and inducing synaptic plasticity.
source: MVR has been suggested to serve a wide range of functions, including enhancing synaptic reliability, controlling synaptic integration, enhancing efficient information transmission by complex spikes, and inducing synaptic plasticity (Rudolph et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rudolph et al., 2015.

claim: The regulatory mechanisms and spatiotemporal organization of MVR events within individual synaptic AZs are poorly understood.
source: However, despite the prevalence and functional significance of MVR, the regulatory mechanisms and spatiotemporal organization of MVR events within individual synaptic AZs are poorly understood.
evidence: This represents the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: Nanoscale co-clustering of presynaptic docking factors and vesicle release machinery has underscored the idea that vesicles are released from relatively stable 'release sites'.
source: Indeed, we know relatively little about the functional organization of vesicle release within the AZ in general—be it related to UVR or MVR events—although findings of nanoscale co-clustering of presynaptic docking factors and vesicle release machinery (Bademosi et al., 2016; Glebov et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2016; Weyhersmüller et al., 2011) have underscored the idea that vesicles are released from relatively stable 'release sites'.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to nanoscopy studies.

claim: The AZ is extremely small and thus beyond the resolution limits of conventional experimental approaches.
source: Progress toward this end is hampered by the fact that the AZ is extremely small and thus beyond the resolution limits of conventional experimental approaches (Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Schikorski and Stevens, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a known technical limitation.

claim: A nanoscale imaging modality is capable of resolving the locations of individual vesicle release events in active hippocampal synapses in culture with ~27 nm precision.
source: Recently, we were able to overcome this limitation by developing a nanoscale imaging modality that is capable of resolving the locations of individual vesicle release events in active hippocampal synapses in culture with ~27 nm precision (Maschi and Klyachko, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: There are multiple, distinct release sites within individual AZs, at which vesicle fusion occurs repeatedly in response to action potentials.
source: Using these tools, we uncovered the presence of multiple, distinct release sites within individual AZs, at which vesicle fusion occurs repeatedly in response to action potentials.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work cited in the text.

claim: Release events were evoked using 1 Hz stimulation for 120 s.
source: Release events were evoked using 1 Hz stimulation for 120 s (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental protocol.

claim: Robust detection of individual release events was achieved at 40 ms/frame rate throughout the observation time period.
source: Robust detection of individual release events was achieved at 40 ms/frame rate throughout the observation time period.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the imaging parameters.

claim: Release sites were defined using a hierarchical clustering algorithm with a cluster diameter of 50 nm.
source: Release sites were defined using a hierarchical clustering algorithm with a cluster diameter of 50 nm (Maschi and Klyachko, 2017) and are shown by crossed circles.
evidence: This is a methodological detail shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Over 90% of fusion event pairs that are involved in MVR were separated by less than 600 nm.
source: Over 90% of fusion event pairs that are involved in MVR were separated by less than 600 nm.
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The average bouton-to-bouton distance is an order of magnitude larger than the average event-to-event distance.
source: The chances of misidentifying two events in the neighboring boutons as occurring in the same bouton is negligible, as we have previously used 3D FIB-SEM reconstruction of our neuronal cultures to show that the average bouton-to-bouton distance is an order of magnitude larger than the average event-to-event distance (Maschi and Klyachko, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous FIB-SEM work.

claim: Synaptic release probability is a strong predictor of a propensity for MVR.
source: Previous studies suggest that the synaptic release probability is a strong predictor of a propensity for MVR (Christie and Jahr, 2006; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AZ size is a major determinant of synaptic release probability.
source: Moreover, we know that AZ size is a major determinant of synaptic release probability (Holderith et al., 2012; Matz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Boutons at which at least one MVR event was observed had a significantly larger AZ than the synapse population overall.
source: Boutons at which at least one MVR event was observed had a significantly larger AZ (Figure 1D and Table 1; N = 3781 (UVR) and 245 (MVR) events, 90 dishes from 11 independent cultures; p<0.001, two-sample KS-test)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Boutons at which at least one MVR event was observed had a significantly larger number of release sites than the synapse population overall.
source: and a significantly larger number of release sites than the synapse population overall (Figure 1E; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: MVR events are more likely to occur at boutons that have larger AZs and higher overall release probability.
source: These results suggest that MVR events are more likely to occur at boutons that have larger AZs and higher overall release probability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing correlation between AZ size, number of release sites, and MVR occurrence.

claim: Full overlap with UVR was observed for ~15% of MVR events.
source: We found full overlap with UVR for ~15% of MVR events, whereas ~47% of MVR events showed partial overlap, and ~38% showed no overlap (Figure 1F; Table 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ~47% of MVR events showed partial overlap with UVR events.
source: We found full overlap with UVR for ~15% of MVR events, whereas ~47% of MVR events showed partial overlap, and ~38% showed no overlap (Figure 1F; Table 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ~38% of MVR events showed no overlap with UVR events.
source: We found full overlap with UVR for ~15% of MVR events, whereas ~47% of MVR events showed partial overlap, and ~38% showed no overlap (Figure 1F; Table 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Release sites can be involved in both UVR and MVR events, but the likelihood that they are involved in one versus the other is not uniform.
source: This observation suggests that release sites can be involved in both UVR and MVR events, but that the likelihood that they are involved in one versus the other is not uniform (explored in more detail below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap data presented.

claim: MVR is a relatively low probability event (~10% of release events are MVR under the experimental conditions used).
source: MVR is a relatively low probability event (~10% of release events are MVR under our experimental conditions), making much longer recordings necessary to determine whether sites are never involved in MVR; indeed, infinitely long recordings are required to answer this question definitively.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations in the study.

claim: Of the two release sites involved in a given MVR event, the one more proximal to the AZ center was significantly more likely to be also involved in UVR events than the more distal site.
source: We found that this probability was location-dependent: of the two release sites involved in a given MVR event, the one more proximal to the AZ center was significantly more likely to be also involved in UVR events than the more distal site (Figure 1G; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The probability that a given release site was involved in both UVR and MVR events formed a gradient from AZ center to periphery.
source: Thus, the probability that a given release site was involved in both UVR and MVR events formed a gradient from AZ center to periphery, supporting the notion of heterogeneity of release site properties across a single AZ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial analysis of release site usage.

claim: Both release sites engaged in an MVR event had a significantly higher release probability than other equidistant, non-MVR-involved release sites in the same bouton.
source: We observed that both release sites engaged in an MVR event had a significantly higher release probability than other equidistant, non-MVR-involved release sites in the same bouton (Figure 1H; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Release sites are highly heterogeneous in terms of release probability, which varied ~5 fold among release sites within the same AZ during the observation time.
source: First, release sites were highly heterogeneous in terms of release probability, which varied ~5 fold among release sites within the same AZ during the observation time (Pr-site range [0.008–0.042]).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of release probability at individual sites.

claim: There is a spatial gradient of Pr-site, which decayed with distance from the AZ center.
source: Second, we observed a spatial gradient of Pr-site, which decayed with distance from the AZ center (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There is a marked heterogeneity of release site properties within the individual AZs, characterized by a gradient of Pr-site from the AZ center to the periphery.
source: Taken together, these findings provide evidence of a marked heterogeneity of release site properties within the individual AZs, characterized by a gradient of Pr-site from the AZ center to the periphery.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Release sites that have a higher propensity for MVR are characterized by a higher release probability than other sites equidistant to the AZ center.
source: These results further suggest that, in addition to the radial distribution of release probability, release sites that have a higher propensity for MVR are characterized by a higher release probability than other sites equidistant to the AZ center.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 1H.

claim: At 2 mM extracellular Ca+2 and at 37°C, over 90% of the events in hippocampal neurons are UVR.
source: At 2 mM extracellular Ca+2 and at 37°C, over 90% of the events in hippocampal neurons are UVR (Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Maschi and Klyachko, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MVR events represent ~9% of all release events in the study.
source: On the basis of this analysis, we estimated that in our studies, MVR events represent ~9% of all release events.
evidence: This is based on amplitude analysis of fusion events.

claim: ~50% of MVR events could be robustly identified as MVR based solely on their amplitude.
source: Of these events, we were able to robustly identify ~50% as MVR based solely on their amplitude (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on amplitude analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The MVR event populations identified by amplitude-based and mixture-model fitting approaches are partially overlapping (~20%).
source: This approach does not rely on spatial information, and thus is complementary to the mixture-model fitting approach that we used above; the MVR event populations that were identified by these two approaches are partially overlapping (~20%; data not shown).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two detection methods.

claim: Distributions of asymmetry scores for the single and double events indicate that they represent two distinct populations.
source: Distributions of asymmetry scores for the single and double events indicate that they represent two distinct populations (Figure 2C; Table 1) and thus validate our approach to robustly distinguish unresolved MVR events from UVR events.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Unresolved MVR events preferentially have smaller asymmetry scores and thus tend to occur at smaller separation distances.
source: First, we observed that unresolved MVR events preferentially have smaller asymmetry scores (Figure 2D) and thus tend to occur at smaller separation distances, similarly to the resolved MVR events (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: More asymmetrical (more spatially separated) unresolved MVR events occurred closer to the AZ center, whereas symmetrical events tend to be more peripheral.
source: We observed that more asymmetrical (more spatially separated) events occurred closer to the AZ center, whereas symmetrical events tend to be more peripheral (Figure 2E, top).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Resolved MVR events show a similar relationship between asymmetry and distance to AZ center as unresolved MVR events.
source: An equivalent calculation for the resolved MVR events (see figure legend for details) showed a very similar relationship (Figure 2E, bottom), supporting the notion that the two subpopulations of MVR events have similar spatial properties.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The extent of overlap of MVR and UVR events at individual release sites was comparable between unresolved and resolved MVR events.
source: The extent of overlap of MVR and UVR events at individual release sites was comparable between unresolved and resolved MVR events (Figures 2F and 1F), with overlap more likely occuring closer to the AZ center in both cases (Figures 2F and 1G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figures 2F and 1F.

claim: Unresolved and resolved MVR events have comparable spatial features.
source: These data suggest that unresolved and resolved MVR events have comparable spatial features.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of spatial properties between the two MVR populations.

claim: The observations can be generalized across the entire population of MVR events.
source: Thus, our observations can likely be generalized across the entire population of MVR events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between resolved and unresolved MVR events.

claim: Previous studies present evidence of temporal 'jitter' on a millisecond timescale (~1–5 ms) within the release pair comprising an MVR event at both excitatory and inhibitory cerebellar synapses.
source: Previous studies present evidence of temporal 'jitter' on a millisecond timescale (~1–5 ms) within the release pair comprising an MVR event at both excitatory and inhibitory cerebellar synapses (Auger et al., 1998; Auger and Marty, 2000; Crowley et al., 2007; Malagon et al., 2016; Rudolph et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: One of the two fusion events comprising an MVR is often noticeably larger in amplitude than the other.
source: Upon initial inspection of resolved MVR events, we noticed that one of the two fusion events comprising an MVR is often noticeably larger in amplitude than the other (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The difference in amplitude within MVR events reflects imperfect synchronization between the two release events.
source: Thus, considering the quantal nature of fusion events, we hypothesized that this difference in amplitude reflects imperfect synchronization between the two release events (if one release event occurs later in the recording frame, we would expect to collect a smaller number of photons for this delayed event, i.e., smaller amplitude) (Figure 3A, top).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation and the experimental setup.

claim: The larger amplitude event (assumed to occur first) was more likely to occur closer to the AZ center than the smaller one in the pair.
source: We observed that the larger amplitude event (assumed to occur first) was more likely to occur closer to the AZ center than the smaller one in the pair (Figure 3B; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The average distance to the AZ center was significantly shorter for the larger amplitude event relative to the event with the smaller amplitude within the pair.
source: Accordingly, the average distance to the AZ center was significantly shorter for the larger amplitude event relative to the event with the smaller amplitude within the pair (Figure 3C; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The amplitude difference within MVR pairs was correlated with the distance between the two events within the pair.
source: Most importantly, this amplitude difference was correlated with the distance between the two events within the pair (Figure 3D,E), such that larger amplitude differences were associated with larger separation distances (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Larger amplitude differences were associated with larger separation distances within MVR pairs.
source: Most importantly, this amplitude difference was correlated with the distance between the two events within the pair (Figure 3D,E), such that larger amplitude differences were associated with larger separation distances (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The uncertainty in determining the fusion event amplitude is ~10%.
source: We note that a component of the amplitude differences can arise from the uncertainty in determining the fusion event amplitude; we estimated this uncertainty to be ~10% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The maximal time difference between the two events comprising MVR is estimated to be less than ~4 ms for the majority of MVR events.
source: Given the observed amplitude differences within the release pairs comprising an MVR event, and the acquisition duration of 40 ms per frame, we estimated the maximal time difference between the two events comprising MVR to be less than ~4 ms for the majority of MVR events in our recordings.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the amplitude differences and frame acquisition time.

claim: The maximal time delay is estimated to be ~2 ms if the measurement uncertainty is factored in.
source: We note that this value overestimates the true extent of desynchronization because, as noted above, a component of the amplitude difference arises from uncertainty in the amplitude measurement itself. Thus, we estimate the maximal time delay to be ~2 ms if the measurement uncertainty is factored in.
evidence: This is an estimate that accounts for measurement uncertainty.

claim: The estimated time delay values are in close agreement with previous reports, which found desynchronization within individual MVR events to be in the range of 1–5 ms.
source: These values are in a close agreement with previous reports, which found desynchronization within individual MVR events to be in the range of 1–5 ms (Auger et al., 1998; Auger and Marty, 2000; Crowley et al., 2007; Malagon et al., 2016; Rudolph et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Vesicle diameter did not exhibit any measurable change as a function of distance from the AZ center.
source: Vesicle diameter did not exhibit any measurable change as a function of distance from the AZ center (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), indicating that the amplitude differences that we observed are not due to systematic differences in vesicle size.
evidence: This is supported by LaSEM analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The amplitude differences observed are not due to systematic differences in vesicle size.
source: Vesicle diameter did not exhibit any measurable change as a function of distance from the AZ center (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), indicating that the amplitude differences that we observed are not due to systematic differences in vesicle size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the vesicle size analysis.

claim: The vGlut1-pHluorin signal amplitude did not measurably change as a function of distance from the AZ center.
source: The vGlut1-pHluorin signal amplitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) did not measurably change as a function of distance from the AZ center, suggesting that a gradient of cleft pH is unlikely to explain the differences in MVR event amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A gradient of cleft pH is unlikely to explain the differences in MVR event amplitude.
source: The vGlut1-pHluorin signal amplitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) did not measurably change as a function of distance from the AZ center, suggesting that a gradient of cleft pH is unlikely to explain the differences in MVR event amplitude.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pHluorin signal analysis.

claim: The average release event amplitude is indistinguishable between events located at the AZ center versus those in the periphery.
source: Indeed, this notion is highlighted by the fact that, in our measurements, the average release event amplitude is indistinguishable between events located at the AZ center versus those in the periphery (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, insert).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B insert.

claim: The observed differences in amplitude within the release pair comprising an MVR event are unlikely to result from a bias in AZ position relative to the imaging plane.
source: Thus, we conclude that the observed differences in amplitude within the release pair comprising an MVR event are unlikely to result from a bias in AZ position relative to the imaging plane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the random orientation of synapses and the lack of amplitude gradient.

claim: Vesicle release associated with MVR is desynchronized and follows a specific spatial organization with respect to the center of the AZ.
source: In summary, our results support the notion that vesicle release associated with MVR is desynchronized and follows a specific spatial organization with respect to the center of the AZ.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the temporal and spatial analysis of MVR events.

claim: The first of the two events in the MVR pair is preferentially located closer to the AZ center.
source: Specifically, the first of the two events in the MVR pair is preferentially located closer to the AZ center.
evidence: This is based on the amplitude and spatial analysis of MVR events.

claim: The probability of observing double events does not increase during the stimulus train.
source: However, we detected no increase in the double event probability during the stimulus train (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The probability of observing double events is slightly higher for the first stimulus, for which there is no preceding stimulation.
source: In fact, the probability of observing double events is slightly higher for the first stimulus, for which there is no preceding stimulation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of double event probability across the stimulus train.

claim: The amplitude distribution of MVR events appears as a single Gaussian peak centered at ~2 q value.
source: Thus, the amplitude distribution of MVR events should appear as a single Gaussian peak centered at ~2 q value (twice the amplitude of a UVR event), as indeed is the case in our measurements (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Single asynchronous release events have a skewed non-Gaussian amplitude distribution shifted towards smaller values than those produced by a full-size synchronous event.
source: As a result, single asynchronous release events are acquired for a wide range of durations that are less than a full frame, and thus must have a skewed non-Gaussian amplitude distribution shifted towards smaller values than those produced by a full-size synchronous event. We confirmed that this is the case using asynchronous events that we recorded in 3 mM Sr2+ in otherwise identical conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The double events in the recordings are synchronous events and have properties that are distinct from those of asynchronous release.
source: Thus, we conclude that the double events in our recordings are synchronous events and have properties that are distinct from those of asynchronous release.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of amplitude distributions.

claim: Asynchronous release events detected in the same frame in the same bouton did not exhibit the spatiotemporal patterns evident for the double events.
source: The asynchronous release events detected in the same frame in the same bouton (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) did not exhibit the spatiotemporal patterns evident for the double events (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and Figure 3D.

claim: The spatiotemporal properties of the double events are distinct from those of asynchronous events.
source: The fact that the spatiotemporal properties of the double events are distinct from those of asynchronous events supports our conclusion that the double events in fact reflect instances of MVR.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of spatiotemporal properties.

claim: Previous studies find minimal asynchronous release evoked by 1 Hz stimulation under nearly identical experimental conditions (37°C, 2 mM extracellular Ca2+).
source: Finally, we note that previous studies find minimal asynchronous release evoked by 1 Hz stimulation under nearly identical experimental conditions (37°C, 2 mM extracellular Ca2+) (Raingo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raingo et al., 2012.

claim: Double events in the recordings reflect synchronous MVR events, with no significant contribution of asynchronous release.
source: Thus, at least five complimentary lines of evidence strongly suggest that double events in our recordings do indeed reflect synchronous MVR events, with no significant contribution of asynchronous release.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented.

claim: Release site usage is regulated in an activity-dependent manner, such that site usage shifts towards the periphery during trains of activity.
source: Our previous study suggested a possible role of calcium in the spatial regulation of release site properties because we observed that release site usage is regulated in an activity-dependent manner, such that site usage shifts towards the periphery during trains of activity (Maschi and Klyachko, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The propensity for MVR events increases as extracellular calcium levels increase.
source: Previous studies have also found that the propensity for MVR events increases as extracellular calcium levels increase (Leitz and Kavalali, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leitz and Kavalali, 2011.

claim: EGTA does not directly affect vesicle release because it is too slow to buffer rapid calcium rise near voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs).
source: EGTA does not directly affect vesicle release because it is too slow to buffer rapid calcium rise near voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), but it is effective in buffering the ensuing slower calcium elevation caused by diffusion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EGTA's buffering kinetics.

claim: EGTA is effective in buffering the slower calcium elevation caused by diffusion.
source: EGTA does not directly affect vesicle release because it is too slow to buffer rapid calcium rise near voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), but it is effective in buffering the ensuing slower calcium elevation caused by diffusion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EGTA's buffering kinetics.

claim: In the presence of EGTA, the amplitudes of the two fusion events comprising MVR were still different, but the difference no longer depended on their separation distance.
source: First, EGTA affected MVR event desynchronization: although the amplitudes of the two fusion events comprising MVR were still different, the difference no longer depended on their separation distance (Figure 4A,B; Table 1; N = 225 synapses, from 57 dishes from 11 independent cultures).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: In the presence of EGTA, a larger proportion of MVR events occurred at shorter intra-event distances.
source: Second, in the presence of EGTA, a larger proportion of MVR events occurred at shorter intra-event distances (Figure 4C; Table 1), that is, pairs of release events comprising MVR were more likely to be closer to each other in the presence of EGTA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The average distances from both events in the MVR pair to the AZ center were significantly shortened in the presence of EGTA.
source: In addition, the average distances from both events in the MVR pair to the AZ center were significantly shortened in the presence of EGTA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Calcium buffering causes MVR events to occur at shorter separation distances and more proximal to the AZ center.
source: Thus, calcium buffering causes MVR events to occur at shorter separation distances and more proximal to the AZ center.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EGTA experiments.

claim: The preferential localization of the larger (earlier) event in the MVR pair closer to the AZ center was still observed in the presence of EGTA.
source: However, the preferential localization of the larger (earlier) event in the MVR pair closer to the AZ center was still observed in the presence of EGTA (Figure 4D, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Several major spatiotemporal features of MVR events are determined, in part, by calcium diffusion following an action potential.

claim: MVR events exhibit non-uniform patterns of spatial and temporal organization that parallel the center-to-periphery organization of release site release probability.
source: We took advantage of our ability to detect individual release events at central synapses with nanoscale precision to reveal three major findings: (i) release sites within the same AZ have highly heterogeneous properties, reflecting a gradient of release probability that decreases from the AZ center to periphery; (ii) MVR events exhibit non-uniform patterns of spatial and temporal organization that parallel the center-to-periphery organization of release site release probability;
evidence: This is a summary of major findings from the study.

claim: Both the gradient of release site properties and the spatiotemporal features of MVR are determined, in part, by the intraterminal calcium elevation following an action potential.
